summary.title: Private Share
summary.description: Self-hosted secret sharing with browser-side AES-256-GCM encryption. The decryption key lives only in the URL fragment; the server stores ciphertext, burns secrets on first retrieval and files on first download, and expires everything after 30 days. Optional Google SSO with guest links (FEATURE_AUTH) and chunked encrypted file uploads (FEATURE_FILE_UPLOADS).

diagrams.title: Private Share data flow
diagrams.description: Secret and file sharing flows across browser, application host, data tier and third parties.

data.name: Sender
data.description: Creates a secret (text and/or file). Anonymous when FEATURE_AUTH is off, Google SSO user or guest-link holder when on.

threats.title: Share link intercepted in transit to the recipient
threats.description: The full link carries both the secret ID and the decryption key (#fragment). Anyone who sees it (chat logs, email archives, forwarded messages, shoulder surfing) can open it before the recipient. The recipient only notices after the fact (secret already burned).
threats.mitigation: Accepted risk (inherent to link-based sharing): whoever holds the full link holds the secret. Mitigations are the optional password sent over a second channel (protected by the per-client backoff and per-secret cap) and burn after reading, which makes an interception visible to the recipient.

threats.title: Instance abused as an anonymous dead drop or malware host
threats.description: Content is opaque to the server, so the instance's domain can be used to distribute phishing text or malware files. Text secrets can be created anonymously even when FEATURE_AUTH is on (see Secrets API).
threats.mitigation: With the Authentication feature on, secret creation and uploads require a signed-in user or a valid guest session, so outsiders cannot use the instance. With the feature off the instance is public by design (operator choice). Content scanning is impossible by design (E2E). Residual: creator attribution in logs is still missing (see Secrets API).

data.name: Recipient
data.description: Opens the share link, optionally enters the password, decrypts in the browser.

threats.title: Recipient denies having viewed the secret
threats.description: A recipient may claim they never received the content.
threats.mitigation: SecretRetrieved logs secret id, client IP and age at retrieval time; the secret is burned and later visits show 'not found'.

data.name: Guest-link holder
data.description: External person who received a signed guest link from an authenticated user. Gets a session-only guest grant until the link expires.

threats.title: Guest link forwarded or replayed by third parties
threats.description: A guest link is reusable by anyone, any number of times, until it expires (GUEST_LINK_TTL_HOURS, default 24). There is no revocation endpoint. EnsureAuthenticated trusts guest_link_id/guest_link_expires_at stored in the session and never re-checks the guest_links row, so deleting the row (or the creating user, which cascades) does not end active guest sessions.
threats.mitigation: Guest links are single-use: opening one (GET) only shows a confirmation, and 'Continue as guest' (POST, signed, CSRF-protected) consumes it with one conditional UPDATE on used_at, so a forwarded or replayed link is refused (410). Consuming on POST keeps mail scanners that prefetch links from burning it. Existing links without used_at work once more after the deploy.

data.name: Operator
data.description: Whoever deploys and runs the instance (env, keys, database, storage, logs).

threats.title: Malicious or compromised operator reads secrets
threats.description: Browser E2E only holds if the served JavaScript is honest. An operator (or anyone controlling the host) can ship JS that exfiltrates keys/plaintext, read secret passwords in transit (they are sent to the server in plaintext), read file names/mime types/sizes in the database, and brute-force the weak 8-char keys offline.
threats.mitigation: Accepted risk: whoever runs the instance or controls its host controls the JavaScript that performs the encryption, so no in-app control can stop them (a compromised server would also serve its own CSP). This is why the README asks users to self-host. Dependency supply chain is tracked separately under Browser SPA.

threats.title: Production deployed with local/debug settings
threats.description: APP_ENV=local with APP_DEBUG=true would register /auth/debug-login (log in as a dev user without SSO), show Laravel debug pages with env values, and trust every proxy.
threats.mitigation: Debug login route is only registered when app()->isLocal() && app.debug, and the controller re-checks. Production error responses always render the branded Error page and only surface HttpException messages. Deployment checklist: APP_ENV=production, APP_DEBUG=false, SESSION_SECURE_COOKIE=true.

data.name: Browser SPA (React + Web Crypto)
data.description: Inertia/React app. Generates the share key, encrypts text (AES-256-GCM, PBKDF2-SHA256 100k) and files (8 MB chunks, per-chunk IV derived from a base IV), decrypts on view, renders markdown.

threats.title: Share key has too little entropy
threats.description: generateKey() produces 8 characters from a 62-symbol alphabet (~47.6 bits). Anyone holding a ciphertext (database leak, backup, log of request bodies, malicious operator) can brute-force it offline; PBKDF2 at 100k iterations only adds ~17 bits of work. OWASP Cryptographic Storage Cheat Sheet expects keys of at least 128 bits.
threats.mitigation: generateKey() now returns a 128-bit key (16 bytes from crypto.getRandomValues, base64url, 22 chars), out of reach of offline brute force regardless of the PBKDF2 iteration count. Legacy 8-char keys are still accepted by isValidKey() so old links keep working; they disappear with the 30-day expiry, after which the legacy pattern can be removed.

threats.title: Share key generated with Math.random()
threats.description: Math.random() is not a CSPRNG; its internal state can be predictable, which further weakens the key.
threats.mitigation: Key bytes come from crypto.getRandomValues (CSPRNG).

threats.title: Stored XSS through markdown secrets
threats.description: Sender-controlled markdown is rendered as HTML in the recipient's browser, which also holds the decryption key in the URL.
threats.mitigation: marked output is sanitized with DOMPurify before rendering; non-markdown content is rendered as text by React. Keep DOMPurify current and add a CSP as defense in depth.

threats.title: Remote resources in markdown track the recipient
threats.description: DOMPurify keeps . A sender can embed a tracking pixel that reveals the recipient's IP, user agent and viewing time to a third-party server.
threats.mitigation: img-src only allows the app, data:/blob: and Google avatars, so remote images in markdown secrets are not loaded and cannot act as tracking pixels.

threats.title: Decryption key persists in browser history and synced tabs
threats.description: The key stays in the address bar after viewing (history.replaceState only updates state, not the URL). Browser history, sync, session restore and screenshots keep a copy. The ciphertext is burned, so impact is limited to cases where a copy of the ciphertext exists (backups, race, DB leak).
threats.mitigation: After a successful decryption the viewer calls history.replaceState to drop the #key fragment from the address bar and the current history entry. The key stays until decryption succeeds so the retry flow keeps working.

threats.title: Clickjacking of the reveal flow
threats.description: No X-Frame-Options / CSP frame-ancestors header is sent. An attacker page can frame /{secret} and trick a user into clicking reveal (burning the secret) or into interacting with the creation form.
threats.mitigation: AddSecurityHeaders sends X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN and CSP frame-ancestors 'self' on every response (OWASP Clickjacking Defense Cheat Sheet).

threats.title: Missing browser security headers
threats.description: The app sets no Content-Security-Policy, Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy or Permissions-Policy (OWASP HTTP Headers Cheat Sheet). Without CSP, any injection or compromised dependency can exfiltrate keys freely.
threats.mitigation: AddSecurityHeaders sends X-Frame-Options, nosniff, Referrer-Policy: no-referrer, Permissions-Policy and a full CSP (nonce-based script-src, restricted img/font/connect/form sources, object-src 'none', base-uri 'self'). HSTS belongs to the TLS edge (README 'Going Live').

threats.title: Compromised frontend dependency or build pipeline
threats.description: Any malicious npm package bundled into the SPA runs with access to keys and plaintext.
threats.mitigation: Layered: Composer and npm refuse releases younger than 3 days; AGENTS.md 'Upgrading Dependencies' requires reviewing lockfile diffs and running composer/npm audit on every upgrade; the full CSP blocks injected inline scripts and pins every data channel (fetch, images, fonts, forms) to known origins. Accepted residual: code already shipped in the bundle can still navigate the page to another site with the key in the URL, which CSP cannot prevent.

threats.title: Plaintext lingers on the recipient device
threats.description: Decrypted content stays in the DOM, JS memory and possibly the clipboard (copy button) after viewing.
threats.mitigation: Accepted risk: once decrypted, content stays in the open tab (and the clipboard if copied) until the recipient closes it; auto-clearing would hurt usability more than it protects.

threats.title: Malicious file name or mime type from sender
threats.description: Name and mime type of a downloaded file come from the sender.
threats.mitigation: Files are delivered as Blob downloads via an anchor download attribute; browsers sanitize file names and never render the blob inline.

data.name: Web pages (Laravel + Inertia)
data.description: GET /, /login, /{secret}, /guest/{guestLink}, auth routes. Shares auth/branding/feature props.

threats.title: Link preview bots burn secrets
threats.description: Chat apps and mail scanners fetch links automatically.
threats.mitigation: GET /{secret} only renders the page (no-store); content is fetched with a POST after an explicit click, so unfurlers do not burn the secret.

threats.title: Secret existence and creation time visible without the key
threats.description: GET /{secret} returns createdAt for any valid ID, without the key or password.
threats.mitigation: Accepted risk: the secret id has ~71 bits of entropy, so only someone who already holds the link learns that it exists and when it was created.

threats.title: Session cookie sent without Secure flag
threats.description: SESSION_SECURE_COOKIE is unset by default, so the session and remember-me cookies can travel over plain HTTP if the site is ever reached without TLS.
threats.mitigation: config/session.php defaults secure to true unless APP_ENV=local; SESSION_SECURE_COOKIE can still override it.

threats.title: Session fixation on guest access
threats.description: GuestLinkController::access writes the guest grant into the existing session without regenerating the session id.
threats.mitigation: GuestSessionController::store regenerates the session id before granting guest access.

threats.title: Inline branding CSS injection
threats.description: Branding values are printed unescaped into a <style> tag.
threats.mitigation: BrandingService only accepts 6-digit hex colors or known Tailwind palette names; anything else falls back to defaults. Values come from env, not users.

threats.title: Error pages leak internals
threats.description: Stack traces or exception messages could reveal paths, queries or env.
threats.mitigation: Outside local env every 4xx/5xx renders the Error page and only HttpException messages are surfaced; JSON requests get standard Laravel errors.

threats.title: Unencrypted appearance cookie tampered
threats.description: The appearance cookie is excluded from encryption.
threats.mitigation: It is only shared to the view as a theme hint and not echoed into HTML.

data.name: Secrets API
data.description: POST /api/secrets, GET /api/secrets/{id}/check, POST /api/secrets/{id}/retrieve. Stores ciphertext, gates on bcrypt password, burns on retrieval.

threats.title: Anonymous secret creation when Authentication is enabled
threats.description: EnsureAuthenticated only guards GET /. POST /api/secrets is open to anyone, so an instance restricted to an organisation can still be used by outsiders.
threats.mitigation: POST /api/secrets runs EnsureAuthenticated: with the Authentication feature on, only signed-in users and holders of a valid guest session can create secrets (401 otherwise, including API clients without a session). Check and retrieve stay public for recipients. Covered by tests/Feature/FeatureAccessTest.php and the guest/user browser tests.

threats.title: Burn-after-reading race returns content twice
threats.description: retrieve() reads the content, then SecretRetrieved deletes the row. Two concurrent requests can both read before either deletes, defeating the single-view guarantee.
threats.mitigation: Secret and SharedFile use the BurnsAfterReading trait: a single DELETE ... WHERE id = ? decides the winner and only the request that removed the row serves the content; the loser gets 404 already_viewed / already_downloaded. Applies to secret retrieval and to both file download paths (signed URL and local). Covered by tests/Unit/BurnAfterReadingTest.php.

threats.title: Online brute force of secret passwords
threats.description: Passwords may be 4 characters. Limits are 5/min per IP+secret and 20/min per IP, so a distributed attacker (or a single one if client IPs are misresolved behind a proxy) can keep guessing until the 30-day expiry. The attacker also needs the share key to read the content, which limits this to people who already have the link.
threats.mitigation: SecretPasswordAttempts: per client (account, or IP with IPv6 collapsed to its /64) five free failures, then lockouts of 1, 2, 4... minutes capped at one day; failures are remembered on a sliding 24 h window and are not reset by successful retrievals. Independently, the tenth wrong password on a secret (from any clients) locks that secret for the rest of the hour, which stops attackers rotating IPs; the trade-off is that a recipient can be locked out for up to an hour. Locked requests are refused before the password is checked and answer 429 with a human wait time shown in the viewer. Remaining: minimum password length is 4.

threats.title: Secret password is not bound to the ciphertext
threats.description: The password is only a server-side gate: it is sent to the server in plaintext and bcrypt-hashed, but the ciphertext is decryptable with the URL key alone. A database leak or the operator bypasses it, and the server sees users' passwords (risky if reused).
threats.mitigation: Accepted risk: the password is a second, server-side layer on top of the 128-bit URL key, not the primary protection. With strong keys a database leak no longer exposes content even without the password.

threats.title: File metadata disclosed before password check
threats.description: check() returns the original file name, mime type and size to anyone with the secret ID, without key or password. The file name is stored in plaintext server-side.
threats.mitigation: Accepted risk: name, mime type and size are needed to show the download before retrieval and are low value compared to file contents. Revisit if instances start sharing files whose names are themselves sensitive.

threats.title: Anyone with the secret ID can burn it
threats.description: retrieve() needs no proof of key, so whoever obtains the ID (log line, partial link, cross-site POST since anonymous API calls have no CSRF token) can destroy the secret.
threats.mitigation: Accepted risk: requires the unguessable id (i.e. the link); a proof-of-key retrieval token is not worth the complexity.

threats.title: Storage exhaustion through mass secret creation
threats.description: 30 requests/min per IP with up to 1 MB of content each, with no global or daily cap. Also, content is validated at 1 MB but the column is TEXT (64 KB on MySQL), so large secrets fail with 500s.
threats.mitigation: Accepted risk: creation is throttled at 30/min per client and, with the Authentication feature on, restricted to signed-in users and guests. Text secrets live in the database and files on the configured disk (S3 in production deployments); watching storage growth and costs is an operational concern for the operator's monitoring, not the app. The content column is MEDIUMTEXT so the 1 MB validation limit is the real limit on MySQL.

threats.title: Secret ID enumeration
threats.description: Attacker iterates IDs to find live secrets.
threats.mitigation: IDs are 12-character Str::random values (CSPRNG, ~71 bits) and routes are throttled at 30/min per IP. Content is still encrypted with the URL key.

threats.title: Mass assignment on secrets
threats.description: Extra fields in the request body.
threats.mitigation: Only validated fields are passed to Secret::create and $fillable is explicit.

threats.title: Secret creation not attributable
threats.description: Creation logs only the secret id: no IP, user id or guest link id, so abuse cannot be traced.
threats.mitigation: AddLogContext (web and api groups) adds request_id, user_id and guest_link_id to every log line written while serving the request, including 'Secret created'.

threats.title: Expired secrets survive when the scheduler is down
threats.description: Expiry is enforced only by the daily secrets:cleanup command; nothing rejects older secrets at read time.
threats.mitigation: Secret::resolveRouteBindingQuery refuses secrets older than Secret::LIFETIME_DAYS (30) at read time; secrets:cleanup deletes them using the same constant.

threats.title: CSRF against session-authenticated API calls
threats.description: Cross-site requests riding the user's session.
threats.mitigation: Sanctum EnsureFrontendRequestsAreStateful applies CSRF verification to first-party requests; session cookie is SameSite=Lax; the SPA sends X-CSRF-TOKEN.

data.name: Files API
data.description: POST /api/files/initiate, /{upload}/chunk, /{upload}/complete (auth:sanctum) and POST /api/files/{file}/download (public). Assembles encrypted chunks and serves or signs the ciphertext once.

threats.title: File download bypasses the secret password
threats.description: /api/files/{id}/download needs no auth, password or token. Anyone who learns the file id (uploader, network logs, a recipient's devtools) can download the ciphertext and burn the file. The file also stays downloadable for up to 30 days if the recipient retrieves the text but never downloads.
threats.mitigation: The download route requires a relative signed URL (signed:relative) that is only issued by a successful retrieve(), valid 24 hours; the first download burns the file, so it works once. A file id alone answers 403. Covered by tests in SharedFileTest.

threats.title: No rate limiting on file and guest-link endpoints
threats.description: /api/files/* and /api/guest-links have no throttle, contrary to the project rule that every endpoint is rate limited.
threats.mitigation: Every route is throttled through the RateLimit enum (per account when signed in, per IP otherwise): uploads 30/min per user (initiate/complete) and 1000 chunks/min (about 1 Gbit/s), guest links 10/min, downloads 30/min, sign-in 10/min, guest access 30/min, pages 120/min. tests/Feature/RateLimitCoverageTest.php fails if a route without a limiter is added.

threats.title: Disk exhaustion through chunk uploads
threats.description: Chunk size is not validated (PHP allows 100 MB per request), total_chunks is unbounded and bytes received are only compared to the declared size at complete(). Pending temp files live 24 h and unattached SharedFiles 30 days, with no per-user quota.
threats.mitigation: Uploads are bounded end to end: the declared size is capped at FILE_MAX_SIZE_GB and must match the chunk count; each chunk is at most 8 MB + tag and the running total cannot exceed the declared size; UploadQuota reserves the declared size per user or guest link against FILE_DAILY_QUOTA_GB (default 100 GB per 24 h) when the upload starts; chunks are throttled at 1000/min; only signed-in users and guests they invited can upload; abandoned uploads are purged within 24 h. Covered by tests/Feature/UploadQuotaTest.php.

threats.title: File uploads accepted while the feature is off
threats.description: The FileUploads flag is only checked when rendering the home page; the API routes only require auth.
threats.mitigation: Upload routes require both the Authentication and FileUploads features through Pennant EnsureFeaturesAreActive (404 when inactive). Download stays available so already-shared files can still be fetched.

threats.title: Pending upload hijacked by another user
threats.description: chunk/complete do not check who initiated the upload. UUIDv4 ids are unguessable, so exploitation needs a leaked id.
threats.mitigation: pending_uploads records the uploader (user_id, or guest_link_id for guest sessions); EnsureUploadOwner answers 404 on chunk/complete to anyone else, including other guests and users. Uploads in flight during the deploy have no owner and expire within 24 h.

threats.title: Concurrent chunks corrupt the assembled file
threats.description: The expected-index check and append are not atomic, so parallel requests for the same index can both append.
threats.mitigation: Accepted risk: only reachable by the upload's own (now verified) owner with a modified client; AES-GCM tags make any corruption fail at decryption.

threats.title: Content-Disposition built with addslashes
threats.description: The sender-controlled file name is placed in the header with addslashes, which does not handle non-ASCII names correctly.
threats.mitigation: Local downloads use Laravel's response()->download(), which encodes the name per RFC 6266 (quoted-string escaping, filename* for non-ASCII). The frontend fallback parser understands both forms.

threats.title: Path traversal through file names
threats.description: A crafted original name used as a path.
threats.mitigation: Storage and temp paths are server-generated UUIDs; the original name is never used in a path.

threats.title: Signed download URL reused or leaked
threats.description: Cloud signed URLs live 5 minutes and can be used repeatedly by anyone holding them; the object is deleted 10 minutes later by a queued job.
threats.mitigation: Accepted risk: signed URLs live 5 minutes and point at ciphertext; they are only handed to the recipient who just retrieved the secret, and the object is deleted 10 minutes later. (The lifetime only bounds when a download may start; a transfer already running continues, so shortening it would not break slow downloads either.)

threats.title: File lost if the local download is interrupted
threats.description: On the local disk the original is deleted before the response is sent, so a failed transfer loses the file.
threats.mitigation: Accepted risk: burn-after-reading deletes the file before it is streamed on the local disk driver; S3 deployments are unaffected because the browser downloads from the bucket.

threats.title: Malware distributed via encrypted files
threats.description: Files are opaque ciphertext, so the server cannot scan them.
threats.mitigation: Accepted risk (inherent to end-to-end encryption): the server cannot scan content it cannot read. Uploads require a signed-in user from an allowed Workspace domain or a guest session from a single-use link one of them issued; uploads are rate limited (guests per guest link) and every upload and secret is attributable in the logs to the user or guest link.

threats.title: File name written to application logs
threats.description: SharedFileObserver::created logs original_name, breaking the rule that logs hold only IDs, timestamps and IPs. File names often contain personal or sensitive information.
threats.mitigation: SharedFileObserver no longer logs original_name (covered by SharedFileModelTest).

data.name: Auth (Google SSO + guest links)
data.description: Socialite Google login with an optional email regex allowlist, logout, signed guest links, EnsureAuthenticated middleware.

threats.title: Email allowlist bypass via weak regex
threats.description: AUTH_ALLOWED_EMAILS takes free-form regexes. An unanchored pattern like /@example\.com/ also matches someone@example.com.attacker.tld, which an attacker can register as a Google Workspace domain.
threats.mitigation: Regex patterns are gone: AUTH_ALLOWED_DOMAINS lists exact Google Workspace domains. GoogleAccountPolicy requires a verified email whose domain is listed and whose hd claim equals that domain (Workspace-managed, not a personal account using a company address). Misconfiguration fails closed: empty list, leftover AUTH_ALLOWED_EMAILS or any non-domain entry keeps sign-in closed and logs an error.

threats.title: Removed users keep access through remember-me
threats.description: Every login uses remember: true and the allowlist is only checked at login, so a user removed from the allowed domain or from Google Workspace keeps access until the remember cookie expires.
threats.mitigation: Accepted risk: sign-in keeps remember-me; access is re-evaluated only at the next Google sign-in.

threats.title: OAuth login CSRF / code injection
threats.description: An attacker logs the victim into the attacker's account, or replays an authorization code.
threats.mitigation: Socialite's stateful driver validates the state parameter; the session is regenerated after login.

threats.title: Guest link signature forgery
threats.description: Crafting a guest URL without a valid link.
threats.mitigation: The signed middleware checks an HMAC with APP_KEY and the id is 32 random characters. Rotating APP_KEY invalidates all links.

threats.title: Account takeover via the Google account
threats.description: A compromised Google account grants app access.
threats.mitigation: Out of scope: relies on the identity provider's MFA and account security.

threats.title: Sign-in and guest links available while Authentication is off
threats.description: Disabling FEATURE_AUTH used to hide only the login page: Google redirect/callback, guest link access and guest link creation stayed routable, so anyone could still sign in (if Google credentials were configured) and reach file uploads.
threats.mitigation: All Authentication routes (login, Google redirect/callback, guest access, guest link creation) and the upload routes sit behind Pennant EnsureFeaturesAreActive, which returns 404 when the feature is inactive. Covered by tests/Feature/FeatureAccessTest.php.

data.name: Scheduler + queue worker
data.description: Daily secrets:cleanup (secrets/files over 30 days, pending uploads over 24 h) and the DeleteStorageObject job for cloud downloads.

threats.title: Cloud objects orphaned when the queue is down
threats.description: For cloud disks the SharedFile row is deleted at download and the object deletion is queued. If the job fails or no worker runs, the object stays forever: the cleanup command only walks database rows.
threats.mitigation: Accepted risk: the production deployment runs a supervised queue worker and objects are ciphertext. Optional backstop: an S3 lifecycle rule expiring shared-files/ after 30 days.

threats.title: Retention not enforced when the scheduler is down
threats.description: Without schedule:run, nothing expires.
threats.mitigation: Expired secrets are refused at read time regardless of the scheduler; files are only reachable through a 24 h signed URL issued by retrieving a live secret. The scheduler still does the physical deletion.

data.name: Database
data.description: secrets (ciphertext, bcrypt password, shared_file_id), shared_files (plaintext name/mime/size, salt, IV), pending_uploads, users, sessions, guest_links, cache, jobs.

threats.title: Database or backup leak enables offline decryption
threats.description: Ciphertexts and salts are stored; with ~47-bit keys they are brute-forceable offline. Burned secrets can also survive in backups and binary logs.
threats.mitigation: Keys are 128-bit since the share-key change, so leaked ciphertexts cannot be brute-forced. Residual exposure: secrets created with legacy 8-char keys until they expire (max 30 days) and plaintext file metadata (accepted, see Secrets API). Keep backup retention short and encrypted at rest.

threats.title: Secret password hashes cracked
threats.description: Leaked password hashes are attacked offline.
threats.mitigation: bcrypt with 12 rounds via the hashed cast.

threats.title: SQL injection
threats.description: Injected SQL through IDs or inputs.
threats.mitigation: Eloquent parameter binding everywhere; secret route parameter constrained to [A-Za-z0-9]{12}.

threats.title: Sessions readable in the database
threats.description: SESSION_ENCRYPT is false, so session payloads (guest grants, flash messages) are readable by anyone with DB access.
threats.mitigation: session.encrypt is hard-coded to true, so session payloads are encrypted with APP_KEY in any store.

threats.title: Bucket misconfigured as public
threats.description: A public or listable bucket exposes every stored ciphertext.
threats.mitigation: Accepted risk (deployment concern): storage privacy is configured outside the app and depends on the FILE_DISK driver. README 'Going Live' > File storage explains it: local disk stays outside the web root; S3-compatible buckets stay private with public access blocked, least-privilege credentials on shared-files/, CORS GET only from APP_URL, optional 30-day lifecycle rule. Stored files are ciphertext either way.

threats.title: Stored ciphertext tampered
threats.description: Someone with storage access alters a file.
threats.mitigation: AES-GCM authenticates every chunk; tampering makes decryption fail in the browser.

data.name: Local temp storage
data.description: storage/app/private/uploads/{uuid} (assembling chunks) and system temp copies served by local downloads.

threats.title: Temp copies left behind after crashes
threats.description: Assembling uploads and download copies stay on disk if a request dies; the uploads dir is created 0755.
threats.mitigation: secrets:cleanup runs hourly: uploads idle for over an hour (by last chunk) are deleted with their chunk file, chunk files without an upload row and local-download copies older than an hour are swept, and the chunk directory is kept 0700. Contents are ciphertext either way.

data.name: Application logs
data.description: Laravel log channel: secret created/retrieved/deleted, shared file created/deleted.

threats.title: Personal data kept in logs
threats.description: Recipient IPs (and today file names) are logged with no defined retention.
threats.mitigation: Accepted risk (deployment concern): client IPs, user ids and guest link ids are logged on purpose for abuse response; file names, content, keys and passwords never are. Retention and rotation are set by whoever runs the instance (log channel or the platform's log pipeline).

threats.title: Logs tampered or deleted
threats.description: Local log files can be edited by anyone with host access.
threats.mitigation: Accepted risk (deployment concern): only someone with host access can alter local logs, and they could do worse; shipping logs to an append-only external sink is an operator choice when logs are needed as evidence.

threats.title: Log injection
threats.description: User input forging log lines.
threats.mitigation: Only server-generated values go in structured Monolog context arrays.

data.name: Cloud storage endpoint
data.description: S3/GCS endpoint the browser downloads from with a signed URL.

data.name: fonts.bunny.net
data.description: Third-party font CSS loaded by every page.

threats.title: Third-party font CDN without SRI
threats.description: The stylesheet is loaded without Subresource Integrity, and every visit leaks the visitor's IP to the CDN (GDPR).
threats.mitigation: Accepted risk: fonts cannot be self-hosted; the CDN serves CSS and fonts only, never scripts.

threats.title: Guest link endpoint not rate limited
threats.description: /guest/{guestLink} has only the signed middleware.
threats.mitigation: Throttled at 30/min per client (RateLimit::GuestAccess).

threats.title: Traffic intercepted without TLS enforcement
threats.description: The app does not enforce HTTPS or send HSTS; TLS depends on the deployment.
threats.mitigation: Accepted risk (deployment concern): TLS termination, the HTTP to HTTPS redirect and HSTS belong to the reverse proxy, load balancer or CDN in front of the app, as described in README 'Going Live' > HTTPS. The app helps by defaulting session cookies to Secure outside local.

threats.title: Rate limits keyed on the wrong client IP
threats.description: TrustProxies is only configured for local. Behind a load balancer or CDN in production every request shares the proxy IP, so all users share one rate-limit bucket (a single client can lock everyone out) and per-IP brute-force protection is meaningless. Trusting '*' instead would let clients spoof X-Forwarded-For.
threats.mitigation: Outside local, config/trustedproxy.php reads TRUSTED_PROXIES (IPs/CIDRs or PRIVATE_SUBNETS) and defaults to trusting none, so X-Forwarded-For is ignored unless the operator lists their proxies; '*' is explicitly discouraged because it makes the leftmost, client-controlled entry the client IP. README 'Going Live' tells operators to configure it. Covered by tests/Feature/TrustedProxiesTest.php.

threats.title: API responses cached by intermediaries
threats.description: check/retrieve JSON responses carry no explicit Cache-Control: no-store (only the page response does).
threats.mitigation: PreventResponseCaching (api middleware group) sets Cache-Control: no-store, private on every API response, including POSTs and file downloads.
